Agree a two-minute review with two questions only: what actually happened, and what would a kind observer say. Then a physical switch. Practice on the last event the client replayed.

fields.label: The event I keep replaying
What I replay most (a sentence, a look, a pause)
My two-minute review: what actually happened
What a kind observer would say
My switch when the two minutes are up
How long the replay used to last, and how long it lasted this time

title: Social Prediction Log
summary: Records the client's forecast before a social situation and the outcome after, to compare over weeks.
goal: Build the client's own evidence that their predictions run far worse than events.
body_md: The forecast must be specific and rated: they will notice me blushing and think less of me, seventy percent. Afterward the client records what observably happened, not how it felt. Review the gap across ten entries, which is usually where belief shifts rather than in any single event.

fields.label: The upcoming situation
What I predict will happen, specifically
How sure I am (0-100%)
What observably happened
How I know (what people said or did)
How the prediction compared
What I predict next time, adjusted

title: Conversation Toolkit Card
summary: A pocket card of openers, follow-up questions and graceful exits for social situations.
goal: Reduce the load of inventing conversation so the client can practice being in it.
body_md: Build it with the client's own words, not scripts from a book, and include exits, since knowing they can leave makes staying easier. Warn against using it as a safety behavior: the card is for learning, and the goal is to need it less. Rehearse a full opener-question-exit in session.

fields.label: Three openers I could actually say
Three follow-up questions that work in most conversations
Two ways to leave a conversation gracefully
What I will do with my hands
The one I will try first this week
How it went, and whether I needed the card

title: Social Brave Steps for Teens
summary: A teen's own ladder of social situations from easy to hard, with a brave step per week.
goal: Give a teenager a graded, self-chosen path back into the social situations they have been dodging.
body_md: Let the teen build and order the steps; a ladder chosen by an adult will not be climbed. Keep parents to a support role agreed on the sheet. Steps should be specific: ask one question in class, not participate more. Celebrate attempts, not outcomes, and expect a step to be repeated before moving up.

fields.label: Situations I have been avoiding
My ladder, easiest at the bottom
This week's step
What I am afraid will happen
What actually happened
What my parent will do (and not do) to help
The step for next week

title: Continuing Bonds Letter
summary: A letter to the person who died, about what has happened since and what the client still carries of them.
goal: Support an ongoing connection with the person rather than a closing of the door.
body_md: Offer it as one option among several, since some clients find writing to the dead unbearable and others find it the only thing that helps. Frame the bond as something that changes rather than ends. The client decides whether to read it aloud, keep it, or take it somewhere. Include 988 among the prompts for the darkest hours.

fields.label: What I want to tell you about since you died
What I have kept of you (a habit, a phrase, an object, a way of seeing)
What I wish I had said
What I think you would say to me now
How I will keep you in my life going forward
If the grief ever gets dangerously dark: 988 (call or text), and who else I will reach

title: Grief Triggers Calendar
summary: A year at a glance with the dates, seasons and events likely to bring the grief up hard.
goal: Let the client see the hard days coming and plan support for them instead of being ambushed.
body_md: Include the obvious dates and the sideways ones: the first snow, the tax season the person used to handle, the song at the store. Plan for the week before an anniversary, which is often worse than the day. Decide with the client who will know about each date.

fields.label: Anniversaries and birthdays
Seasons, holidays and rituals that will be different
Sideways reminders I can predict
The next hard date, and what I will do that day
Who will know it is coming
What helped on the last hard date, and what did not

title: Dual Process Week Planner
summary: A week planned with time for facing the loss and time for the ordinary business of living, both on purpose.
goal: Normalize moving between grief and daily life instead of feeling guilty about either.
body_md: Explain that healthy grief moves between the loss and the rest of life, and that neither side is avoidance. Clients stuck on one side feel guilty when they laugh, or numb when they cannot cry; the planner gives both permission. Keep the entries small and concrete.

fields.label: Times this week I will let myself be with the loss (looking at photos, visiting, talking about them)
Times this week I will do ordinary or even pleasant things
The side I tend to get stuck on
What guilt says when I switch sides
What I will say back to it
How the week went

title: Memory Box Project
summary: A child decorates a box and fills it with objects, drawings and stories that hold the person who died.
goal: Give a grieving child a concrete, permitted place for their memories and a way to talk about them.
body_md: Let the child lead on what goes in and what stays private. Each item comes with a story the child tells if they want to; the telling is the work. Involve the surviving parent or carer where possible, and coach them to follow the child's pace rather than their own. Revisit the box on hard dates.

fields.label: What my box looks like
The first three things I put in it, and why
A story that goes with one of them
Something I want to ask about the person who died
Who I can open the box with
When I might want to open it

title: Grief Conversation Cards
summary: A deck of gentle prompts about the person who died, drawn in turn by family members or a group.
goal: Let a family or group talk about the person in a structured, low-pressure way.
body_md: Write the prompts with the group first so nothing on a card ambushes anyone, mixing light ones with heavier ones. Any card can be passed. Play in a circle with a talking object. In families, children often answer more freely than adults, which gives the adults permission.

fields.label: Prompts we put on the cards
The card I drew, and what I said
Something I learned about the person from someone else
A card I passed on
The card I would like to answer next time

title: Needs Inventory for Partners
summary: Each partner lists their needs in the relationship, ranked, and guesses their partner's list before comparing.
goal: Replace assumed needs with stated ones, and show each partner what the other has been guessing.
body_md: Have both partners complete it separately, including the guess about each other, before any discussion. The gaps between the guess and the real list are the material. Keep the tone of curiosity when a partner's need surprises the other; surprise is information, not an accusation.

fields.label: My top five needs in this relationship, ranked
How well each is being met right now (0-10)
What I think my partner's top five are
What surprised me about their real list
One need of theirs I could meet better this month
One need of mine I will ask for directly

title: Perpetual Problems Sorter
summary: Sorts a couple's recurring arguments into the solvable and the perpetual, and plans a different approach to each.
goal: Stop a couple from trying to solve what needs managing, and from managing what could be solved.
body_md: List the arguments first, then sort. Perpetual problems come from differences in personality or values and will be there in ten years; the goal is dialogue and humor about them, not a fix. Solvable problems get a concrete plan. Most couples are relieved to hear that having perpetual problems is normal.

fields.label: Arguments we have more than once a month
Which of these come from a difference in who we are
Which could actually be solved with a plan
For one solvable problem: our plan
For one perpetual problem: what we can each accept
How we will talk about the perpetual one next time it comes up

title: Trust Rebuilding Steps
summary: A shared ladder of specific, observable actions that would rebuild trust after a breach, with a timeline.
goal: Turn a vague demand to earn trust back into steps both partners can see happening.
body_md: The hurt partner names what would help; the other partner says what they can commit to. Steps must be observable, since promises to change are not. Agree how long the checking phase lasts, because trust cannot rebuild under permanent surveillance. Review progress monthly in session.

fields.label: What was broken, in one sentence each
Actions that would help me trust again (specific and visible)
Which of these I can commit to, and when
What transparency looks like for now, and for how long
What I need to hear when I have a wobble
How we will mark progress

title: Communication Pattern Replay
summary: Replays one recent exchange line by line, with each partner naming what they meant and what they heard.
goal: Show a couple the gap between what was said, what was meant and what landed.
body_md: Pick a short exchange, not the biggest fight. Write the actual lines, then have each partner add what they meant and what they heard. The gaps are usually where the fight lives. Finish by rewriting two lines each, and rehearse the rewrite in session.

fields.label: The exchange, line by line, as it happened
For my lines: what I meant
For their lines: what I heard
Where the gap between meant and heard was widest
Two lines I would rewrite
How the rewritten version sounds out loud

title: Relationship Values Compass
summary: Each partner names the kind of partner they want to be, separately from how the other is behaving.
goal: Anchor each partner to their own values so change does not wait on the other person moving first.
body_md: Works with a couple or with one partner alone. The key move is separating my values as a partner from what I get back; clients often discover they have been acting on a scoreboard. Choose one valued action for the week that does not depend on the other person's response.

fields.label: The partner I want to be, in three words
How I have actually been acting lately
What I have been waiting for my partner to do first
One valued action I will take this week regardless
What my mind says will happen if I go first
What actually happened

title: Safety and Stabilization Plan
summary: A plan for the practical and emotional safety a survivor needs in place before any deeper work.
goal: Put steady ground under the client first: who, where, what, and what to do when it gets too much.
body_md: Complete it together in session and never as homework. Cover present-day safety from the person who harmed them, the people who help, the skills that bring them back, and what to do in the worst hours. Move at the client's pace and do not ask for the details of what happened; that is not what this sheet is for. Include 988.

fields.label: Am I safe from the person now? What would make me safer
People I trust, and what each one can help with
Skills that bring me back when I am flooded
Signs that I am doing too much too fast

What I want my therapist to know about pace
What I am not ready to talk about yet, and that is fine

title: Consent and Boundaries Map
summary: Maps the client's yes, no and maybe across touch, closeness and conversation, in their own words.
goal: Help a survivor reclaim the right to decide, in small everyday ways, what they allow and what they do not.
body_md: Keep it to everyday boundaries at first: hugs, sitting close, questions from family, who has their number. The maybe column matters, since survivors often feel boundaries must be absolute to count. Rehearse one no in session. Nothing here asks about the abuse itself.

fields.label: Things I am a clear yes to
Things I am a clear no to
Things that are a maybe, and what would make them a yes
A boundary someone in my life keeps crossing

What I will do if they push

title: Shame Response Sheet
summary: Catches the self-blame that follows abuse, tests it against what the client would say to another survivor, and writes the fairer version.
goal: Loosen the belief that the client caused, allowed or deserved what happened.
body_md: Do this in session, gently, and expect the double standard to be stark: the client will extend to another survivor a compassion they refuse themselves. Do not argue the client out of the belief; let the comparison do the work, and rate belief before and after. Stop if the client becomes flooded and return to grounding.

fields.label: What I tell myself about why it happened
How much I believe that (0-100%)
What I would say to a friend who told me the same story

title: Support Disclosure Planner
summary: Plans whether, who, when and how much to tell, so a disclosure happens on the client's terms.
goal: Keep the choice of who knows, and how much, in the survivor's hands.
body_md: Not telling is a valid outcome of this sheet and should be said out loud. Work through what the client wants from telling, who is likely to respond well, and how much to say; a first sentence and an exit line are worth rehearsing. Plan for the reaction being disappointing, since it sometimes is.

fields.label: What I hope telling someone would give me
People I might tell, and how I think each would respond
The person I would tell first, if anyone
How much I want to say (a sentence is enough)
My first sentence
How I will end the conversation if I need to
What I will do for myself afterward, whatever their reaction

title: Body Safety Rules Poster
summary: A child makes a poster of body safety rules: private parts, okay and not-okay touch, secrets versus surprises, and who to tell.
goal: Teach a child the words and the permission to tell, as part of prevention work with families.
body_md: A prevention and education tool, done with a parent in the room where possible. Use correct names for body parts. Teach that surprises are fun and short and secrets about bodies are never kept. List five trusted adults. If a child discloses during this, stop the activity, stay calm, believe them, and follow your mandated reporting duties.

fields.label: Private parts have proper names, and mine are
Okay touch and not-okay touch: my examples
The difference between a surprise and a secret
My five trusted grown-ups
What I say if someone breaks a body safety rule
Where my poster will hang

title: Coping Menu by Situation
summary: A menu of the client's coping options sorted by where they are: at work, in public, at home, in bed.
goal: Match skills to settings so the right one is available where the distress actually happens.
body_md: Most clients have skills that only work at home and distress that happens elsewhere. Sort by setting and check that each setting has at least two options that are invisible to other people. Include one for the middle of the night. Keep the menu in the phone's notes.

fields.label: At work or school: two things I can do without anyone noticing
In public: two options
At home: two options
In bed at 3 a.m.: two options
The skill I reach for too often, and where it does not work
The new skill I will try this week, and where

title: Skill Practice Log
summary: A weekly log of which coping skill the client used, in what situation, and how well it worked.
goal: Turn coping from a vague resolve into a tracked practice with results.
body_md: The rating is the useful part: a skill that scores three out of ten in three different situations can be retired without guilt. Look for the mismatch between skills tried and situations faced. Praise the attempt, especially when the skill did not work, since trying is what builds the habit.

fields.label: Date and the situation
Distress before (0-10)
The skill I used
Distress after (0-10)
How well it worked (0-10) and why
A skill I could have used instead
The skill I will practice most next week

title: Coping Ladder for Kids
summary: A ladder of a child's coping moves from small feelings at the bottom to big ones at the top.
goal: Match the size of the coping move to the size of the feeling, in a picture a child can use.
body_md: Draw a ladder with three or four rungs and let the child assign feelings sizes to each. Small feelings get small moves: a breath, a drink of water. Big feelings get big moves: a break, a grown-up. Practice one move per rung in session and have the parent post the ladder at home.

fields.label: Bottom rung: a small feeling and my small move
Middle rung: a medium feeling and my medium move
Top rung: a huge feeling and my biggest move
How I know which rung I am on
Who helps me on the top rung
Where my ladder is posted

title: Coping Skills Relay
summary: Teams race to act out or demonstrate a coping skill for each situation card drawn.
goal: Rehearse coping skills under mild pressure and laughter, so they are practiced rather than just known.
body_md: Write situation cards with the group beforehand: a test tomorrow, a friend ignoring a text, a loud house. A team scores when the skill fits the situation and could actually be done there. Judge fit, not speed, and let the group argue the call; the argument is the learning.

fields.label: Situation cards we made
Skills my team demonstrated
A skill another team showed that I want to steal
A situation none of us could match well
The skill I will practice this week

title: Helpful vs Costly Coping Sort
summary: Sorts everything the client does to feel better into what helps in the long run and what costs more than it gives.
goal: Help the client judge coping by its long-term workability rather than by how fast it works.
body_md: List everything without judgment first, including the ones the client is ashamed of; those are usually the fastest-acting. Sort by long-term workability, not by how they look. Most clients find a few things belong in both columns depending on amount, which is worth writing down rather than resolving.

fields.label: Everything I do to feel better, fast or slow
Which ones help me next week too
Which ones cost more than they give
Which ones depend on how much
One costly one I will shrink, and how
One helpful one I will do more of, and when

title: Phobia Prediction Tracker
summary: Records what the client expects to happen around the feared object or situation and what actually occurs.
goal: Build the client's own evidence that the feared outcome and the felt danger diverge.
body_md: Ask for the specific feared outcome, not just fear: I will faint, the dog will bite, the plane will crash. Rate belief before and after each approach. The pattern across entries is what changes belief, so aim for at least eight entries before drawing conclusions together.

fields.label: The feared thing and the situation
What I predict will happen, specifically
How sure I am (0-100%)
Peak fear (0-10)
What actually happened
What I did during the peak
My belief in the prediction now (0-100%)

title: Approach Steps Planner
summary: Plans the next approach step toward a feared object in detail: where, how long, with whom, and what to drop.
goal: Make each approach step concrete enough to actually happen this week.
body_md: One step at a time, planned to the minute. Include what safety moves the client will drop, since carrying the escape plan into the step blunts it. Decide in advance how long to stay: long enough for the fear to fall, not just to touch and run. Debrief in session before planning the next.

fields.label: This week's step
Where and when, exactly
Who will be there, and what they will and will not do
How long I will stay (until fear drops by half)
The safety moves I will not use
What happened, and what I will do next week

title: Phobia Body Response Sheet
summary: Names what the client's body does around the feared thing, and separates the alarm from the danger.
goal: Help the client see the fear response as an alarm that can fire without a fire.
body_md: Map the response: heart, breath, muscles, stomach, the urge to run. Explain plainly that the body's alarm is doing its job and that the job is to get them out, which is why staying feels wrong. For blood or needle fears, note the faint response and plan applied tension separately.

fields.label: What my body does first around the feared thing
What it does next
The urge that comes with it
What the alarm is trying to make me do
What I know about the real danger in this situation
What I will do with the alarm next time it fires

title: Brave Practice Chart for Kids
summary: A sticker chart for a child's repeated brave practices with a feared thing, tied to a small reward.
goal: Make repetition of approach steps visible and rewarding for a child.
duration: 20 minutes to set up, then daily
body_md: Choose practices small enough to repeat daily: look at a picture of a dog, stand in the doorway with the lights off. Stickers go on for attempts, not for calm. Parents hold the chart and the reward and keep their own anxiety out of the practice. Change the practice when it stops earning fear.

fields.label: My brave practice this week
Stickers I earned
How scared I was the first time (0-10) and the last time
My reward when the chart is full
What my grown-up does during practice
Next week's brave practice

title: Fear Ladder Card Sort
summary: Situations written on cards and physically sorted into a ladder from least to most scary.
goal: Build a fear hierarchy as a hands-on sorting task rather than a form.
body_md: Write one situation per card with the client, at least fifteen, then sort them on the table or floor. The physical sorting draws out distinctions a form misses, and the client can move cards as beliefs change. Photograph the finished ladder and use it to choose the next approach step.

fields.label: Situations we wrote on cards
The bottom three cards
The top three cards
Cards I moved while sorting, and why
The card I will start with
The card I cannot imagine reaching yet

title: Body Neutrality Practice
summary: Daily short statements about what the body did today rather than how it looked.
goal: Move the client's relationship with their body from judgment toward function and use.
duration: Two minutes daily for two weeks
body_md: Aim for neutral, not positive; clients who cannot believe their body is beautiful can believe it carried them up the stairs. Keep the statements about doing and feeling. Notice when the client sneaks an appearance comment in and gently redirect. Never mention weight, shape or food in this practice.

fields.label: Three things my body did for me today
One thing it let me feel (warmth, music, a hug, the wind)
A neutral statement about my body, without judgment either way
What my mind wanted to add about how it looks
How I responded to that
The statement I will use tomorrow morning

title: Body Checking Log
summary: Records the mirror checks, pinching, comparing and photo scrutiny that keep body worry alive, and what each one did to mood.
goal: Show the client how checking feeds the worry, and plan a reduction.
body_md: Checking feels like getting information but produces worse mood almost every time; the log makes that visible. Include the quiet forms: reflections in windows, comparing in group photos, clothes tried and discarded. Plan one check to cut in half, not to stop entirely.

fields.label: Date and time
What I checked, and how (mirror, pinch, photo, comparing)
What I was looking for
Mood before and after (0-10)
How long the reassurance lasted, if any
The check I will cut in half next week
What I will do instead in that moment

title: Appearance Assumptions Sheet
summary: Lists the client's rules linking appearance to worth, acceptance or success, and tests each one.
goal: Loosen the beliefs that make appearance carry the whole weight of self-worth.
body_md: Draw out the if-then rules: if I looked different, then people would... Test each against the client's own experience and the people they admire. The goal is to shrink the share of self-worth that appearance holds, which a pie chart of what makes up their worth can show before and after.

fields.label: My rules about appearance (if I looked..., then...)
Where each rule came from
Evidence from my own life for and against it
People I admire, and how much their looks have to do with it
How much of my self-worth appearance holds now (%)
What else I would like it to rest on

title: Body Gratitude Function List
summary: A list of what the client's body has carried them through, by life stage, written as a record rather than a rating.
goal: Build a history of the body as a companion rather than an object under review.
body_md: Move through life stages: childhood play, illness survived, work done, people carried, places reached. The tone is a record, not a pep talk. Clients with a history of harming or overworking their body may find this tender; slow down there. No comments on shape or size anywhere on the sheet.

fields.label: What my body did for me as a child
What it has carried me through
What it lets me do that I would miss
Someone it has held or helped
Something it recovered from
What I would like to thank it for, plainly

title: Media Diet Audit
summary: An inventory of the accounts, shows and images the client consumes, and what each does to how they feel in their body.
goal: Change what the client feeds their body image, since much of it arrives through a screen.
body_md: Go through the phone together. For each account or habit, ask what it does to the client's body feeling in the ten minutes after. Unfollowing is a real intervention and often the fastest one; replace, do not just remove, so the feed is not empty. Repeat in a month.

fields.label: Accounts and shows I see most
How I feel in my body after each (better, worse, nothing)
The ones that leave me comparing
Accounts I will unfollow or mute this week
What I will follow instead (bodies doing things, other interests entirely)
How my feed feels after the change

title: Good Enough Standard Setter
summary: A worksheet for setting a good-enough bar for a task before the client starts it.
goal: Use it to loosen an all-or-nothing standard before a task begins.
body_md: Before a task that tends to spiral into overwork, the client writes what good enough would look like, separately from what perfect would look like, then commits in writing to stopping at the good-enough line. Useful right before a paper, a work email, or a cleanup that usually runs long. Revisit afterward: did stopping at good enough cost anything the client actually cares about, or only the discomfort of stopping?

fields.label: The task I'm about to start
What "perfect" would look like here
What "good enough" looks like here
My stopping point, in writing
What happened when I stopped there

title: Session Opening Check-In Card
summary: A short scale-and-prompt card clients fill out before session to start with real data.
goal: Use it to open session with where the client actually is, not a guess.
body_md: Handed over before session starts, this card asks for a quick number and a word rather than a full recap. It gives the clinician something concrete to open with, instead of a generic how-was-your-week question. Some clients rush through it; that itself is useful data about where their attention is. Keep it to the few minutes before the session properly begins, not as take-home work.

fields.label: My mood right now, 0 to 10
One word for this week
What I want to make sure we cover today
Anything since last time worth flagging

title: Weekly Decision Log
summary: A running log of decisions made over the week and the reasoning behind each one.
goal: Use it to surface a client's actual decision-making pattern over time.
duration: Five minutes daily for one week
body_md: Each day the client notes one decision, big or small, what tipped it one way, and how sure they felt afterward. Reviewed together at the next session, the log tends to reveal a pattern, always deferring, always taking the fastest option, always asking three people first, that is easier to see written down across a week than described from memory in the room. Useful before targeting any specific decision difficulty.

fields.label: Decision 1: what I chose and why
Decision 1: how sure I felt after, 0 to 10
Decision 2: what I chose and why
Decision 2: how sure I felt after, 0 to 10
Decision 3: what I chose and why
Decision 3: how sure I felt after, 0 to 10
The pattern I noticed across the week

title: Personal Rulebook Audit
summary: A worksheet that lists a client's unspoken personal rules and tests each one for flexibility.
goal: Use it to make implicit personal rules explicit and open to question.
body_md: Most people carry a private rulebook of always-and-never rules, always answer texts fast, never ask for help, always finish what's started, that they've never written down or questioned. The client lists a handful, rates how rigid each feels, and picks one to loosen on purpose this week. This works well early in longer-term work as a map of where the pressure is coming from, before targeting any single belief directly.

fields.label: A rule I live by that starts with "always" or "never"
Where I think this rule came from
How rigid it feels, 0 to 10
What it costs me to keep it
One small way I could bend it this week

title: Readiness for Change Ruler
summary: A simple 0-to-10 ruler for rating importance and confidence about a specific change.
goal: Use it to locate where ambivalence about a change is actually coming from.
body_md: The client rates a specific change on two separate rulers, how important it feels and how confident they are they could do it, then explains why they picked that number and not one lower. The why-not-lower question tends to surface existing motivation better than asking why not higher does. Low importance and low confidence point to different next conversations, so keep the two scores separate rather than averaging them.

fields.label: The change I'm considering
How important this feels, 0 to 10
Why that number and not lower
How confident I am I could do it, 0 to 10
Why that number and not lower

title: Double Standard Technique
summary: A worksheet that has the client answer their own harsh thought the way they'd answer a friend's.
goal: Use it to expose the gap between a client's self-talk and their compassion for others.
body_md: The client writes down a harsh self-judgment, then imagines a friend saying the exact same thing about themselves and writes the response they'd actually give that friend. Placed side by side, the gap between the two responses is usually obvious to the client without the clinician pointing it out. If the client's answer to the friend is just as harsh, that's useful information too, and worth exploring rather than treating as a failed exercise.

fields.label: The harsh thought, exactly as it runs through my head
A friend who said this exact thing about themselves
What I would actually say back to that friend
How my two answers compare

title: Problem-Solving Steps Card
summary: A step-by-step card that walks a client through defining a problem, weighing options, and picking one.
goal: Use it to slow down problem-solving when a client is stuck cycling on one option.
body_md: Many clients arrive at a problem already fixated on one solution or paralyzed between two. This card forces the sequence: state the problem in one plain sentence, list every option without judging it yet, rate each one quickly, then pick and schedule a first step. The brainstorming step is the one clients most want to skip; hold them to writing at least three options, even bad ones, before any rating happens.

fields.label: The problem, in one plain sentence
Every option I can think of, judgment aside
A quick rating for each option, 1 to 5
The option I'm picking
My first step, and when I'll take it

title: Belief Certainty Thermometer
summary: A rating scale that tracks how strongly a client believes a recurring thought before and after examining it.
goal: Use it to track whether certainty in a recurring thought is actually shifting over time.
body_md: Rather than working through the full evidence-gathering steps each time, this is a quick before-and-after number for a thought the client already knows well. It's most useful once a specific thought has come up in a few sessions and the clinician wants a trend line rather than another full breakdown. A number that isn't moving over several weeks is itself worth naming out loud with the client.

fields.label: The recurring thought
How much I believe it right now, 0 to 100
One piece of evidence that complicates it
How much I believe it after considering that, 0 to 100

title: Self-Instructional Training Script
summary: A written script of coaching self-talk a client rehearses for a specific hard task, step by step.
goal: Use it to build a rehearsed internal script for a task that usually triggers a freeze.
duration: 20 minutes to build, then practiced before the task
body_md: The client writes short coaching lines for themselves at each stage of a specific hard task, before starting, mid-task, if a mistake happens, and after finishing, in their own words rather than generic affirmations. Read it aloud together first; the wording only works if it sounds like the client's own voice and not a script. This pairs well with something concrete and repeatable, like a phone call the client keeps avoiding.

fields.label: The task this script is for
What I'll say to myself before I start
What I'll say to myself partway through
What I'll say to myself if I make a mistake
What I'll say to myself when it's done

title: Point-Counterpoint Thought Debate
summary: A written back-and-forth where the client argues both sides of a stuck negative thought in turn.
goal: Use it to loosen a thought the client can state but can't seem to argue with.
body_md: The client writes one line arguing for the negative thought, then immediately one line arguing against it, alternating several rounds rather than writing a single list of evidence for each side. The back-and-forth rhythm tends to surface weaker arguments for the thought that a straight list doesn't. Running it out loud in session first, with the clinician taking one side, gives the client a model before they try it alone on paper.

fields.label: The thought we're debating
Round 1 — for
Round 1 — against
Round 2 — for
Round 2 — against
Which side held up better, and why

title: Values vs Goals Sorting Cards
summary: A sorting exercise that separates a client's stated values from the specific goals attached to them.
goal: Use it to untangle a value from the goal a client has been chasing in its name.
body_md: The client writes down several things they've been striving toward, then sorts each one into a direction or a destination. A goal can be checked off; a value can't, only lived. Clients who've stalled on an unreachable goal often discover the value underneath it is still fully available to act on today, even with the goal unmet. Keep the sorting concrete, real examples from their week, not abstractions.

fields.label: Something I've been working toward
Is it a direction (ongoing) or a destination (checkable)?
The value underneath it
One way to live that value today, goal aside

title: Value-Action Gap Tracker
summary: A short daily log comparing a client's stated values to what they actually did that day.
goal: Use it to make the gap between stated values and daily action visible over a week.
duration: Five minutes daily for one week
body_md: Each evening the client names one value that mattered to them that day and rates, honestly, how much their actual behavior lined up with it. The point isn't to produce a high score; a string of low ones is exactly the useful data. Bring the completed week into session and look for which value shows the widest gap, that's usually the one worth building committed action around next.

fields.label: A value that mattered today
How much my actions matched it, 0 to 10
What got in the way, if anything

title: Naming the Story Practice
summary: A defusion exercise where a client gives a recurring thought pattern a short name to say instead of arguing with it.
goal: Use it to give a client a fast way to notice a familiar thought pattern without engaging its content.
body_md: Together, name a thought pattern that shows up often, the not-good-enough story, the running-late story, something short enough to say silently in the moment it appears. Practice catching it live in session first: when the thought shows up, the client says there's the story instead of debating the content. This is defusion, not disagreement, so resist the urge to fact-check the story once it's named; naming it is the whole move.

fields.label: The recurring thought pattern
The short name we're giving it
A moment this week I caught it and named it
What I did next instead of arguing with it

title: Feared and Wanted Self Compass
summary: A worksheet contrasting the person a client fears becoming with the person they want to become.
goal: Use it to locate values by contrasting a feared future self with a wanted one.
body_md: The client describes, in some detail, the person they're afraid of becoming if things keep going the way they're going, then does the same for the person they want to become. Values tend to surface more clearly in this contrast than they do from a straight what-matters-to-you question. Keep both descriptions concrete and specific rather than abstract traits, and end by naming one action this week that moves toward the wanted self.

fields.label: The person I'm afraid of becoming
The person I want to become
The value that shows up in that contrast
One action this week toward the wanted self

title: Function Over Form Card Sort
summary: A sorting exercise that classifies a client's behaviors by what they accomplish, not what they look like.
goal: Use it to help a client see that two very different behaviors can serve the same function.
body_md: The client writes down several different behaviors from the week, some that look nothing alike on the surface, and sorts them by the function each one seems to serve: avoiding, connecting, numbing, controlling. Two behaviors that look opposite, like overworking and avoiding a task entirely, often land in the same pile once function is the sorting rule. This works well as a bridge into workability, once the pattern of function is visible on paper.

title: Interpersonal Effectiveness Priorities Sheet
summary: A worksheet for ranking objective, relationship, and self-respect priorities before a hard conversation.
goal: Use it to set clear priorities before scripting a request or a refusal.
body_md: Before building a DEAR MAN script, the client ranks what matters most for this specific conversation: getting the outcome, protecting the relationship, or keeping self-respect intact. All three rarely rank equally, and knowing the order changes how firm or how soft the eventual script should be. This is a quick preparatory step, best done right before drafting the actual script rather than as a standalone exercise.

fields.label: The conversation I'm preparing for

title: Both-And Language Swap
summary: A quick drill that has a client rewrite but-statements as and-statements to practice dialectical thinking.
goal: Use it to practice holding two true things at once instead of picking one.
body_md: The client writes a few sentences from the week that used but to pit two things against each other, I love them but I'm furious, and rewrites each one with and instead. The swap sounds small on paper but changes what the sentence is claiming: not a contradiction to resolve, but two things that are both true. Some clients resist the rewrite because it feels like letting themselves off the hook; that resistance is worth naming.

title: Self-Validation Practice Card
summary: A short practice for a client to validate their own reaction before deciding whether to act on it.
goal: Use it to build the habit of validating a reaction before judging or acting on it.
body_md: Clients who are fluent at validating other people often skip the same step for themselves, moving straight from feeling to self-judgment. This card slows that down: name the reaction, find the piece of it that makes sense given the situation, say it back in plain language, and only then decide what, if anything, to do about it. Validating a reaction is not the same as agreeing it should drive the next action, and that distinction is worth making explicit.

title: Nonjudgmental Stance Practice Card
summary: A drill for rewriting a judgmental thought about a situation into a plain, factual description.
goal: Use it to practice describing a situation before evaluating it as good or bad.
body_md: The client writes a judgmental line from the week, that was a disaster, then rewrites it as a plain description of what actually happened, with no good, bad, should, or shouldn't. Most clients find the factual version surprisingly hard to produce on the first try, which is itself worth naming. This is a rehearsal skill, best practiced on low-stakes moments before the client tries it on something that actually stung.

title: Build Mastery Activity Planner
summary: A weekly planner for scheduling one activity that builds a sense of competence and accomplishment.
goal: Use it to schedule regular activities that build a sense of mastery, not just pleasant ones.
body_md: Separate from pleasant activities, this planner schedules one thing per day that stretches the client slightly and leaves them with a sense of having accomplished something, a skill practiced, a task finished, a small challenge met. Difficulty should be chosen on purpose: too easy and it won't register as mastery, too hard and it won't get attempted. Review at the end of the week for which activities actually landed as a sense of competence.

title: Daily Temperature Reading
summary: A five-part structured check-in ritual couples run at home covering appreciations, updates, and hopes.
goal: Use it to give a couple a low-stakes daily structure for actually talking to each other.
body_md: Each partner takes a turn through five parts in order: something they appreciate about the other, new information about their day, anything confusing they want clarified, a complaint paired with what they'd want instead, and a hope for the future. The fixed order matters; appreciation always goes first, complaints are never allowed without a stated request attached. Couples who skip straight to the complaint step tend to recreate their usual fight, so hold them to starting with appreciation.

title: Curious Questions Interview for Partners
summary: A structured interview where each partner asks the other open questions and only reflects back, no responding.
goal: Use it to practice curiosity between partners without either one defending or fixing.
body_md: One partner asks a series of open questions about a topic, a stress, a hope, a past event, while the other answers; the asking partner's only job is to reflect back what they heard, no advice, no rebuttal, no relating it to themselves. Switch roles halfway through. The hardest part for most partners is resisting the urge to jump in; if that happens, pause and name it rather than letting the interview turn into a normal back-and-forth conversation.

title: Conflict De-escalation Signal System
summary: A worksheet where partners agree in advance on a shared signal to pause a conversation before it escalates.
goal: Use it to build an agreed way to pause a conversation before it turns into a bigger fight.
body_md: Built when both partners are calm, not mid-argument, this sets a specific word, gesture, or phrase either one can use to call a pause, plus what happens next, how long the pause lasts and who restarts the conversation. Vague agreements like just tell me to stop tend not to hold up under real heat; push for something oddly specific enough that it can't be missed or mistaken for part of the argument itself.

title: Money Conversation Starter Cards
summary: A set of low-pressure prompt cards that open up a couple's talk about money and shared spending.
goal: Use it to open a money conversation before it's forced by a bill or a disagreement.
body_md: Money conversations often only happen reactively, after a purchase or a bill has already caused friction. These cards give a couple a lower-stakes way in, questions about what money meant growing up, what feels safe versus risky, what a shared goal might look like, separate from any live disagreement. Run it on a calm evening, not right after a financial argument, and let each partner answer fully before moving to the next card.

title: Shared Play and Fun Inventory
summary: A worksheet that maps out what counted as fun for a couple early on and what still does now.
goal: Use it to rebuild a couple's shared sense of play, not just their problem-solving.
body_md: Couples often narrow down to logistics and repair work in sessions and lose track of whether they still have fun together at all. Each partner separately lists what used to be playful between them, what still is, and one small thing they'd like to try. Compare lists together; overlap is a good place to start scheduling something low-stakes this month, before tackling anything heavier in the next session.

title: Calm-Down Corner Blueprint
summary: A drawing activity where a child designs their own calm-down spot at home, step by step.
goal: Use it to give a child ownership over a specific calm-down space at home.
body_md: The child draws and labels a corner of a room, a beanbag, a soft light, a few chosen items, as their own calm-down spot, then the caregiver helps make it real at home that week. Having the child choose every item themselves matters more than how tidy or correct the drawing looks. Send the caregiver home with the plan and check in next session on whether the spot got built and used.

title: Feelings Traffic Light Craft
summary: A craft where a child builds a traffic light and matches each color to a step for handling big feelings.
goal: Use it to give a child a simple stop-think-go sequence for big feelings.
body_md: The child colors and cuts out a red, yellow, and green circle, then decides with the caregiver what each color means: red for stop and notice the feeling, yellow for a calming strategy, green for going back to what they were doing. Stick it somewhere visible at home so the caregiver can point to a color during a real moment instead of explaining the whole idea from scratch in the heat of it.

title: Coping Skills Robot Build
summary: A craft where a child builds a paper robot with each body part standing for a different coping skill.
goal: Use it to make a set of coping skills into something concrete a child can point to.
body_md: The child assembles a simple paper robot, and each part gets a job: the arms for a hug or squeeze, the lungs for slow breaths, the feet for a walk or stomp, the head for counting or naming colors in the room. Building it together in session lets the clinician check each skill actually makes sense to the child before it goes home. Encourage the caregiver to keep the robot somewhere the child can grab it fast.

title: Kindness Bingo Card
summary: A bingo card of small kind acts a child checks off across the week at home or school.
goal: Use it to build a habit of noticing and doing small kind acts.
body_md: Fill the grid together with small, doable kind acts sized to the child, holding a door, sharing a toy, checking on a sad friend, and let the child color a square each time one happens, with the caregiver helping notice and log it that day. A full card isn't the point; a couple of squares filled by next session is still worth celebrating and naming out loud in the room.

title: Playdough Feelings Sculpt
summary: A sensory activity where a child sculpts a feeling out of playdough and talks about its shape and texture.
goal: Use it to give a child a hands-on way into naming a feeling they can't yet put into words.
body_md: Some children can shape a feeling before they can name it. Hand over playdough and ask them to make what a feeling looks like, big or small, spiky or smooth, one color or several, then talk through the choices they made rather than asking directly what does this mean. Keep the questions about the sculpture itself; naming the feeling often follows on its own once the child has something in their hands to point to.

title: Find Someone Who Icebreaker
summary: A mingling group game where members find who among them matches each prompt on a card.
goal: Use it to open a new group with low-stakes mingling before deeper sharing starts.
body_md: Each member gets a card with several prompts, like find someone who has a pet, or find someone who's tried a coping skill this week, and mingles to fill in a name next to each one before time runs out. Keep the prompts light for a brand-new group and save anything more personal for later sessions once trust has built. Debrief by asking what surprised them or what they have in common with someone they didn't expect.

title: Musical Chairs Check-In Game
summary: A group game where the music stopping cues a quick check-in prompt for whoever's nearest a chair.
goal: Use it to break up a long group session with a light, moving check-in.
body_md: Set up a chair for everyone, no elimination, and play music while the group moves around; when it stops, whoever's nearest a marked chair answers a quick check-in prompt pulled from a stack before the music starts again. Skip the usual elimination rule so nobody sits out; the point is the movement and the prompt, not a winner. Debrief afterward on which prompt was hardest to answer out loud.

title: Four Corners Opinion Game
summary: A group game where members move to a room corner matching how strongly they agree with a statement.
goal: Use it to make a group's range of opinions visible and open a discussion from there.
body_md: Label four corners of the room strongly agree, agree, disagree, and strongly disagree, read a statement aloud, and have everyone move to the corner that fits before any discussion starts. Once everyone's placed, ask a few people in different corners to explain their spot. Statements work best when there's no clear right answer; pull from the group's own week rather than abstract debate topics.

title: Trust Walk Game
summary: A paired game where one partner guides the other, eyes closed, through a safe space using only words.
goal: Use it to build a concrete, felt sense of trust between two people through a shared task.
body_md: One person closes their eyes while their partner guides them slowly through a cleared, safe space using only spoken directions, no touching unless agreed beforehand. Switch roles after a few minutes. Keep the space genuinely obstacle-free and check in before starting about what kind of guidance actually feels helpful versus overwhelming. Debrief on what it was like to depend on someone else's words alone.

title: Coping Skills Speed Match
summary: A timed team game matching coping-skill cards to scenario cards before the clock runs out.
goal: Use it to make recalling and matching coping skills to situations faster and more automatic.
body_md: Split into small teams, each with a stack of coping-skill cards and a stack of scenario cards; on go, teams race to pair each scenario with a skill that could plausibly help before time runs out. There's rarely one right answer, so score for a reasonable match explained out loud rather than a fixed answer key. Debrief on which scenario was hardest to match and why.

title: End-of-Session Grounding Checklist
summary: A short checklist to confirm a client is grounded and safe before they leave a trauma-focused session.
goal: Use it to make sure a client leaves session regulated, not raw, after trauma-focused work.
duration: Five minutes at the end of session
body_md: Run through this checklist at the close of any session that touched trauma-related material: check the client's current arousal level, orient them to where they are and what day it is, confirm a support plan for the next few hours, and name one grounding skill they'll use if activated later. Watch for clients who try to rush out the door once the clock runs low; slow the close down deliberately and treat it as part of the session, not an optional extra.

title: Anniversary Reaction Planner
summary: A forward-looking plan for the dates and seasons that tend to stir up a trauma anniversary reaction.
goal: Use it to help a client line up support and pacing before a known hard date arrives.
body_md: Talk with the client about which dates or seasons tend to bring a spike in symptoms, then build a plan for that window: who they'll tell ahead of time, what they'll lighten on their calendar, and which grounding or support step they'll lean on if the day gets hard. This is planning, not processing, so keep the focus on logistics and support rather than on retelling events from the past. Revisit and update the plan each year, since the dates or the needs around them can shift.

title: Then vs Now Safety Check
summary: A present-moment check comparing an old alarm reaction to the actual safety of right now.
goal: Use it to help a client notice when a threat alarm is firing from then, not now.
body_md: When a client notices their body sounding an alarm, walk them through naming the sensation, then checking concrete present-moment evidence: where they are, who is with them, and what is actually happening right now, separate from what the alarm seems to be warning about. The point isn't to argue the alarm away but to give the client a quick, repeatable way to orient to the present when an old reaction fires in a safe context. Keep it brief and concrete; this is a present-tense check, never a place to write out the original event.

fields.label: What my body is doing right now
What the alarm seems to be warning me about

title: IMPROVE the Moment Card
summary: A card walking through the DBT IMPROVE skills for getting through an overwhelming moment safely.
goal: Use it to give a client a menu of ways to make a hard moment more bearable without escalating.
body_md: Walk the client through the IMPROVE letters, imagery, meaning, one thing at a time, a brief mental vacation, encouragement, and relaxation, and have them mark which ones tend to actually work for their body. Some clients gravitate to one or two letters and never touch the rest, which is fine; the point is a short list they can reach for fast rather than working every letter every time. Practice one or two in session before sending the card home, so the client has felt it work at least once.

Meaning: something that helps this moment make sense

title: Safety Signal System for Couples
summary: A private signal partner A can give when triggered, and a calm response plan for partner B.
goal: Use it to help a couple respond to trauma triggers with pacing instead of confusion or panic.
duration: 30 minutes to set up, then ongoing
body_md: Partner A picks a simple word or gesture to signal feeling triggered or overwhelmed, something easy to use even while flooded. Partner B agrees on a short, predictable response: give space, lower their voice, and stay nearby without pressing for an explanation. Build the plan together in session so neither partner is guessing later, and practice the signal once while both are calm. This is a pacing tool for the moment, not a prompt for either partner to explain or relive what happened.

title: What-If Spiral Tracker
summary: A worksheet for tracing a chain of what-if thoughts to find where the spiral can be interrupted.
goal: Use it to help a client see the shape of a worry spiral instead of getting lost inside it.
body_md: Have the client write the first what-if that started a spiral, then the next thought it led to, and the next, until the chain runs out or gets too big to keep writing. Reading the chain back usually shows how far the mind traveled from the original, small trigger. Ask where in the chain the client could realistically interrupt the spiral next time, often earlier than they'd expect, and circle that link as the target for practice.

title: Probability Overestimation Log
summary: A log comparing a client's predicted odds of a feared outcome against what actually happened.
goal: Use it to correct a pattern of overestimating how likely a feared outcome really is.
body_md: Before a feared situation, have the client write down what they think will happen and their percentage estimate that it will. Afterward, they record what actually happened and re-rate it in hindsight. Most clients with anxiety consistently overestimate the odds; seeing the gap in their own numbers across several entries tends to land harder than being told the odds are lower. Review the pattern together after a week or two rather than pointing it out after a single entry.

title: Anxious Mind Radio Station
summary: A defusion exercise imagining anxious thoughts as a radio station playing in the background.
goal: Use it to help a client notice anxious thoughts without treating each one as an announcement.
body_md: Ask the client to name their anxious inner voice as a radio station, something like Worry FM, that plays whether or not anyone is tuned in. Practice noticing when the station comes on, naming it out loud, Worry FM again, and choosing whether to turn the volume up or let it play in the background while attention goes elsewhere. The goal isn't to turn the station off; it's to change the client's relationship to a broadcast that used to feel like the only channel available.

title: Nonjudgmental Anxiety Narration Card
summary: Practice describing anxious thoughts and sensations in plain facts, without judgment words attached.
goal: Use it to help a client separate raw anxious experience from the judgments piled on top.
body_md: Have the client describe an anxious moment twice: first in their usual language, then again using only observable facts, what the body did, what the thought said, with no words like terrible, stupid, or awful attached. Most clients are surprised how much of their distress comes from the judgment layer rather than the raw sensation underneath it. This is a describing practice, not a debate about whether the anxiety is justified.

title: Worry Detective Badge Kit
summary: A pretend-detective kit for kids to investigate what their worry is trying to warn them about.
goal: Use it to help a child feel curious about worry instead of only scared of it.
body_md: The child becomes a Worry Detective with a badge and a notebook, investigating one worry at a time: what clue tipped them off that worry showed up, what the worry seems to be trying to protect them from, and one brave step to test it out. The caregiver plays sidekick, asking questions rather than answering for the child, and a badge sticker is earned for each brave step attempted, whether or not it goes well. If a child discloses something concerning during the investigation, the clinician's reporting duties apply.

title: Good Enough Task Tiers
summary: A worksheet breaking one task into a bare-minimum, better, and best version for low-energy days.
goal: Use it to help a client finish something on a low day instead of freezing over the ideal version.
body_md: For one task the client keeps avoiding, help them write three versions: the bare minimum that still counts, a better version if there's a bit more energy, and the best version if the day allows it. On a low-energy day the client is only asked to hit the bare minimum tier, no apology needed. This breaks the all-or-nothing pattern where a task feels pointless unless done fully, which for many low-mood clients means it never gets started at all.

title: Anticipated vs Actual Enjoyment Log
summary: A log comparing how much enjoyment a client predicts from an activity against what they actually felt.
goal: Use it to correct the low-mood prediction that nothing will feel worth doing.
body_md: Before an activity, the client rates how much they expect to enjoy it. Right after, they rate what they actually felt. Low mood tends to predict flat or negative in advance and undersell what actually happened, and clients rarely notice the gap unless it's written down side by side. Use a run of entries, not just one, to make the pattern visible, and prompt the client to choose the next activity based on the log rather than the prediction.

title: The Depression Story Sort
summary: A card sort separating the running story low mood tells from the plain facts of the day.
goal: Use it to loosen the grip of a fixed low-mood narrative on how a client reads their own day.
body_md: Write out a handful of statements from the client's inner narrative, such as I never do anything right or nothing will change, on separate cards, then sort them into two piles: story and fact. A fact has to be something a video camera could have recorded; a story is interpretation, however familiar it feels. Most cards land in the story pile, which is the point, not to prove the story wrong, but to show the client it's a story they're carrying, not a verdict.

title: Behavioral Activation Dice Game
summary: A dice game that picks a category of small activity to do right now, with a debrief question after.
goal: Use it to lower the barrier to starting an activity when motivation is too low to choose one.
body_md: Label six dice faces with categories, movement, connection, self-care, mastery, novelty, and rest, and have the client roll. Whatever comes up, they commit to one small action in that category within the next ten minutes, in session if possible. After trying it, ask the debrief question: what changed, even slightly, in mood or energy, once they did it? The game removes the paralysis of choosing among options by making the choice random and small.

title: Daily Mastery Builder Card
summary: A daily card for choosing one small task to complete competently, to counter feelings of helplessness.
goal: Use it to rebuild a sense of competence one small completed task at a time.
duration: Five minutes daily for two weeks
body_md: Each day, the client picks one task slightly on the easier side of their ability and does it as well as they reasonably can, then notes it on the card. The task should be small enough to actually finish, organizing one drawer, replying to one message, not a project. This DBT mastery skill works against the helplessness that low mood builds by giving the client daily, countable proof that they can still do something well, however small.

title: Transition Countdown Planner
summary: A worksheet for building a warning countdown before a hard task switch instead of a sudden stop.
goal: Use it to make transitions between tasks less likely to trigger resistance or a meltdown.
body_md: Map out a transition that reliably goes badly, screen time to homework, play to bedtime, and build a countdown around it: a warning at ten minutes, five minutes, and two minutes, each with a specific phrase or signal rather than a vague almost time. Add one small bridge activity between the two tasks, like a two-minute stretch, so the switch isn't abrupt. Adjust the countdown length based on what the client actually needs, not what seems reasonable on paper.

title: Executive Function Self-Talk Rewrite
summary: A thought record rewriting self-critical labels about forgetfulness into function-based language.
goal: Use it to replace lazy self-talk with language that points to a fixable executive function gap.
body_md: Have the client write the harsh label that shows up after a missed deadline or forgotten task, lazy, careless, broken, next to what actually happened in executive function terms: a working-memory slip, a planning gap, a time-blindness moment. Rewriting the event in function language doesn't excuse the impact, but it opens up a fixable next step instead of a character verdict the client can't act on. Keep a running list of these rewrites to spot the client's most common gap.

title: Body Battery Check-In Cards
summary: Cards a child uses to show their energy and focus level as a battery icon throughout the day.
goal: Use it to help a child and caregiver notice a low-focus dip before it turns into a meltdown.
duration: Five minutes, several times a day
body_md: Give the child a set of battery cards from full to empty and have them pick one at set check-in points, after school, before homework, before bed. A caregiver keeps the check-ins short and judgment-free; the point is information, not a report card. A pattern of afternoon empties, for example, might mean homework moves earlier or a movement break gets built in first. Track the pattern for a week before making changes based on it.

title: Focus Relay Race
summary: A turn-based relay game where each player beats a short timer on one small focus task.
goal: Use it to practice short bursts of sustained focus in a format that feels playful, not draining.
body_md: Set a short timer, ninety seconds works well, and have each player complete one small task before it runs out, sorting cards, a simple puzzle piece, a short copying task, then pass to the next player. Keep tasks genuinely short so success is likely and the timer creates mild urgency rather than pressure. After each round, ask the debrief question: what helped you stay with it for those ninety seconds? Adjust task difficulty and timer length to keep it winnable.

title: ADHD Teamwork Task Map
summary: A map for splitting household follow-through so neither partner ends up as the default rememberer.
goal: Use it to turn follow-through gaps into a shared system instead of a blame cycle.
body_md: Have partner A and partner B list the recurring tasks that tend to get dropped, then sort each one by who's better positioned to own the reminder system for it, not who should remember, but who has a system that actually works for them, like an alarm or a visible list. The partner without ADHD names what support looks like without turning into a reminder service; the partner with ADHD names what kind of reminder actually lands. Revisit the map monthly since what works tends to drift.

fields.label: Task that keeps getting dropped
Who owns the reminder system for it
What kind of reminder actually works for that partner
What support from the other partner looks like, without nagging

title: High-Risk Situation Planner
summary: A worksheet for mapping upcoming situations likely to raise urges and planning for each one ahead of time.
goal: Use it to help a client prepare for risky situations before urges show up, not during them.
body_md: Have the client list specific situations coming up in the next week or month that have raised urges around substance use before, a certain event, a certain person, a certain time of day, and for each one, write a concrete plan: who they'll go with, what they'll say if offered, and an exit option if it gets hard. Planning ahead of time, while the urge isn't active, tends to produce steadier answers than trying to think clearly in the moment. Review the plans together before the situation arrives.

fields.label: The upcoming situation
What tends to raise urges about it
My plan going in
What I'll say if offered
My exit option if it gets hard

title: Urge Thought Record
summary: A thought record capturing the automatic thought that shows up right before an urge to use.
goal: Use it to test the automatic beliefs that make an urge feel more urgent than it is.
body_md: When an urge tied to substance use shows up, have the client write the automatic thought that came with it, often something like I can't handle this or just this once won't matter, rate how much they believed it in the moment, and later, once the urge has passed, rate it again with some distance. Reviewing a run of entries usually shows the belief was more convincing during the urge than it looks afterward, which is useful evidence for the next one.

fields.label: The situation
The automatic thought that came with the urge

What actually happened

title: Urge Willingness Scale
summary: A practice for rating willingness to feel an urge without acting on it, tracked across a scale.
goal: Use it to build a client's capacity to feel an urge fully without needing it to go away first.
body_md: When an urge tied to substance use shows up, have the client rate two things side by side: how strong the urge feels, and how willing they are to let it be there without acting on it, both on a zero to ten scale. The goal isn't to force willingness to ten; it's to notice that the two numbers can move independently of each other, and that willingness tends to rise with practice even when urge intensity doesn't drop. Track a few entries together to make the pattern visible.

fields.label: Urge intensity, 0 to 10
My willingness to feel it without acting, 0 to 10
What I did instead
What I noticed about the two numbers

title: Dialectical Abstinence Planner
summary: A DBT-informed plan holding both a full commitment to stop and a real plan for what happens after a lapse.
goal: Use it to help a client commit fully to change without abandoning the effort after one lapse.
body_md: Have the client write their full commitment to stopping substance use in their own words, then, on the same page, write a specific plan for what they'll do in the first hour after an urge wins out and a lapse happens, who they'll call, what they won't do, how they'll get back to the commitment. Holding both at once, total commitment and a real lapse plan, is the dialectical move: it removes the all-or-nothing trap where one slip to an urge reads as total failure and the whole effort gets dropped.

fields.label: My commitment, in my own words
My plan for the first hour after a lapse, if one happens
Who I'll call
How I'll get back to the commitment

title: Support vs Enabling Conversation Map
summary: A guide helping both partners sort which supportive habits help recovery and which quietly enable use.
goal: Use it to help a couple tell genuine support apart from patterns that protect substance use.
body_md: Have partner A, the partner working on substance use, and partner B, the supporting partner, each list things partner B currently does to help, then sort the list together into support and enabling, covering for missed commitments versus letting natural consequences land when an urge wins out, for example. This conversation tends to bring up guilt on both sides, so keep the tone toward the shared goal rather than blame. Agree on one or two changes to try for a couple of weeks, not a full overhaul at once.

Support or enabling?

title: Anger Recovery Time Log
summary: A log of how long the body takes to settle after anger spikes, tracked across the week.
goal: Use it to spot whether recovery time after anger episodes is shrinking or stuck.
duration: One week, a few minutes per entry
body_md: Most anger work focuses on triggers and warning signs, but how long the body stays activated afterward matters too. Have the client log the time from an anger spike to feeling settled again, along with what helped the comedown. Patterns often show certain settings or people stretch recovery out, and some go-to strategies shorten it fast. Bring the week's entries into session and look for the outliers together, rather than just averaging the numbers.

Time I noticed the spike
Time I felt back to my normal self

What made it take longer

title: Hostile Attribution Recheck
summary: A CBT worksheet that tests a hostile first read of someone's behavior against kinder alternatives.
goal: Use it to slow the jump from an ambiguous situation straight to feeling disrespected.
body_md: Anger often follows a snap judgment that someone meant to be inconsiderate or disrespectful, before any other explanation gets considered. Walk the client through a recent moment that sparked anger: the first, hostile read of what happened, then two or three other explanations that fit the same facts just as well. Rate how angry each version feels on its own. The goal isn't to talk the client out of their anger, but to show how much of the heat comes from the interpretation chosen, not the event itself.

My first read on what happened
A second explanation that also fits the facts

title: Being Right vs Being Effective Check
summary: A DBT-informed check-in that weighs winning the argument against getting what actually matters.
goal: Use it to help a client choose effectiveness over being right in a heated moment.
body_md: Borrowed from the DBT idea of choosing effectiveness over being right, this card gives a client three quick questions to run through mid-conflict: what do I actually want here, does proving my point get me closer to it, and what would the wise-mind version of me do instead. It works best rehearsed calm first, then carried as a card or phone note for the real moment. Some clients resist it at first because being right feels like the whole point; naming that resistance out loud in session usually helps.

fields.label: What I actually want from this situation
Does proving my point get me closer to that?

title: Anger Thermostat Dial
summary: A paper dial a child builds and colors to show how hot their anger is getting right now.
goal: Use it to give a child a hands-on way to notice and turn down rising anger.
body_md: The child cuts out a simple dial and colors zones from cool blue through hot red, then writes or draws one calming move next to each zone, like squeezing a pillow or asking for space. Tape a spare paper arrow on with a brass fastener so it turns. The caregiver's job is to notice out loud when the dial creeps toward red and invite the child to move the arrow themselves rather than announcing how they feel. Keep the finished dial somewhere visible, like a bedroom door, so it becomes a shared cue.

title: Escalation Signal System
summary: A private signal couples agree on ahead of time to flag rising anger before it boils over.
goal: Use it to help partners interrupt escalation earlier than a full blowup.
duration: 20 minutes to set up, then ongoing
body_md: Have each partner name their own early signs of rising anger, then agree together on one word or gesture either of them can use the moment those signs show up, no explanation required in the heat of the moment. The signal's only job is to pause the conversation, not to win it or assign blame. Some couples pick a word, others a hand on the table. Practice using it once in session on a low-stakes disagreement so it doesn't feel awkward the first time it's needed for real.

title: Mental Ritual Tally Sheet
summary: A simple tally for mental rituals like counting, praying, or replaying a moment, not just visible ones.
goal: Use it to bring silent, mental compulsions into view alongside physical ones.
body_md: Mental rituals are easy to miss because there's nothing to see, so clients often undercount them next to hand-washing or checking. Ask the client to carry a small tally sheet and mark a line each time they notice themselves counting, praying, reviewing, or mentally fixing a thought on purpose, without stopping to analyze it in the moment. The running total across a week often surprises people, and the sheet becomes a starting point for choosing one mental ritual to work on directly in session.

title: Thought-Action Fusion Checker
summary: A worksheet that tests the belief that having a thought is as risky as acting on it.
goal: Use it to separate the content of an intrusive thought from its imagined power.
body_md: Many people with intrusive thoughts believe, often without naming it, that thinking something makes it more likely to happen or is morally equal to doing it. Have the client write down a recent intrusive thought, then rate two separate beliefs: how likely the thought is to come true just because they had it, and how much having it says about their character. Compare those ratings to a thought they'd call neutral, like thinking about the weather. Most clients notice the two thoughts aren't held to the same logical standard, which is worth sitting with.

How likely I think it is to come true just from thinking it, 0 to 10

title: Naming the OCD Voice
summary: An ACT defusion exercise that labels intrusive OCD demands as a voice, not a command.
goal: Use it to help a client notice OCD's urgency without automatically obeying it.
body_md: Give the urgency behind an obsession a name, like 'the OCD voice' or a nickname the client picks themselves, so it's easier to notice as one voice among many rather than the whole truth. When an obsession fires, the client silently says 'there's the voice again' instead of arguing with the content or rushing to comply with a ritual. This isn't about proving the voice wrong, which usually fuels more looping; it's about creating a small gap between hearing the demand and acting on it.

title: Just-Right Feeling Practice
summary: A sticker practice where a child leaves something a little imperfect on purpose and rides out the feeling.
goal: Use it to help a child practice tolerating a not-quite-right feeling without fixing it.
duration: Five minutes, a few times a week
body_md: Some children get stuck needing things lined up, matched, or repeated until they feel just right, and fixing the urge in the moment only strengthens it. Pick one small, safe thing to leave imperfect on purpose, like an uneven stack of blocks or a crooked sticker, and set a timer for how long to leave it alone. The child earns a sticker for the practice itself, not for how it feels afterward. The caregiver's job is to stay calm and not fix it either, even if asked, and to point out that the feeling faded on its own.

fields.label: What we left a little imperfect today
How long we set the timer for
How big the not-quite-right feeling was, 0 to 10
How big it was by the end of the timer

title: Uncertainty Dice Challenge
summary: A dice game where each roll hands the client a small, safe uncertainty challenge to sit with.
goal: Use it to practice tolerating uncertainty in a lower-stakes, playful format.
body_md: Before rolling, build a list of six small uncertainty challenges together, ranked roughly easy to harder, like sending a text without rereading it or leaving a room without checking the stove twice. Each number on the die maps to one challenge. The client rolls, completes that challenge before the next session if possible, and rates how tolerable the not-knowing felt afterward, not right away. Roll again for a harder set once the easier challenges stop feeling like a big deal. Close each round with one debrief question.

Number rolled
