title: Panic Aftermath Reset
summary: A short checklist for right after a panic attack passes, before the memory of it gets set.
goal: Use it to help a client reset and reorient in the minutes just after an attack fades.
duration: Five minutes, right after an episode
body_md: Most panic tools focus on the buildup or the middle of an attack, leaving the immediate aftermath unaddressed, which is often when a frightening memory of the episode gets cemented. Right after the peak fades, have the client name three things they can see, take a sip of water, and jot one line about what actually happened versus what they feared would happen. This isn't about analyzing the attack in depth; it's a short reset before returning to whatever they were doing. Bring the collected sheets into session to look for patterns across episodes.

fields.label: Three things I can see right now
What I feared would happen
What actually happened
One word for how I feel right now

title: Panic Safety Behavior Drop-Out
summary: A behavioral experiment that drops one safety behavior at a time to test what actually happens.
goal: Use it to test whether a safety behavior is preventing harm or just preventing discomfort.
body_md: Clients with panic often carry a safety behavior, like gripping a water bottle, sitting near an exit, or checking their pulse, believing it's the only thing keeping a feared outcome from happening. Pick one low-stakes safety behavior and agree on a single outing where the client drops it on purpose, predicting beforehand what they think will happen without it. Afterward, compare the prediction to what actually happened. The point isn't to prove panic won't happen; it's to test whether the behavior was really necessary.

title: Panic Escape Urge Surf
summary: A DBT-style log that tracks the urge to flee a panic attack instead of acting on it right away.
goal: Use it to help a client ride out the urge to escape until it crests and falls.
duration: During an episode, then reviewed weekly
body_md: Borrowing the DBT idea of surfing an urge instead of immediately obeying it, this log has the client rate the urge to leave or escape a situation every couple of minutes during a panic episode, rather than acting on the first spike. Most urges to flee crest within several minutes even when the panic itself takes longer to fully settle. Reviewing the ratings afterward in session shows the client, in their own numbers, that the urge has a shape and an end, which is easy to forget in the moment.

title: Partner Reassurance Boundaries Conversation
summary: A structured talk about how much reassurance around panic actually helps versus keeps it going.
goal: Use it to help partners agree on a reassurance plan instead of improvising in the moment.
body_md: Partners of someone with panic often end up over-reassuring without meaning to, answering the same what-if question many times a day because refusing feels unkind in the moment, even though it tends to keep the worry cycle going. Have each partner name what reassurance currently looks like between them, then agree together on a smaller, specific version, like answering a health worry once and then redirecting to a plan instead of re-litigating it. Revisit the agreement after a couple of weeks since it usually needs adjusting.

title: Panic Alarm Off-Switch Craft
summary: A craft where a child builds a pretend alarm switch and labels it with their own calm-down move.
goal: Use it to give a child a hands-on way to understand panic as a false alarm they can turn off.
body_md: Explain panic to a child as the body's alarm system going off by mistake, like a smoke detector triggered by toast instead of a real fire. The child decorates a paper switch or button, writes one or two body clues next to it that mean the alarm is going off, like a racing heart or shaky hands, and one action next to the switch that helps turn the volume down, like slow breathing or squeezing a stress ball. Keep the craft somewhere the child can point to it. The caregiver's role is to name the false alarm calmly rather than reacting with worry.

title: Sibling Conflict Pattern Log
summary: A log that tracks who, what, and when in sibling conflicts instead of relitigating each one live.
goal: Use it to spot the recurring pattern underneath repeated sibling fights.
body_md: Sibling conflict often gets handled fight by fight, with parents trying to reconstruct who started it in the moment, which rarely goes anywhere useful. Have the parent jot a quick line after each conflict this week: who was involved, roughly what triggered it, time of day, and how it ended, without trying to assign blame on the spot. Bring the log into session and look across entries for the pattern, like a particular time of day, activity, or tired sibling that shows up again and again.

title: Child Behavior Reframe Card
summary: A CBT card that tests a parent's harshest read of a child's behavior against kinder alternatives.
goal: Use it to slow a parent's jump from a child's behavior to a story about their character.
body_md: Parents under stress often land on the harshest available explanation for a child's behavior, like 'he's doing this on purpose to get at me,' and respond to that story rather than to what actually happened. Have the parent write down a recent moment that frustrated them, their first read on why the child did it, and two other explanations that fit the same facts, like tiredness, a skill the child hasn't learned yet, or a need the child can't name. Rate how frustrated each version feels.

title: Family Helper Chart Craft
summary: A chart a child helps design to track family jobs, not just one child's individual rewards.
goal: Use it to give a child ownership over contributing to the family, not just earning points.
body_md: Unlike a chart built around one child's target behavior, this one is about the whole family pitching in. The child helps pick and draw icons for a handful of real household jobs, some theirs and some a parent's or sibling's, and the family moves a marker to whoever did which job that day. There's no prize for finishing; the point is visibility of who's contributing. Parents should resist turning it into a scorecard for arguments and instead use it as a quick, low-drama way to notice when the load has quietly shifted onto one person.

title: United Front Discipline Script
summary: A pre-written script two parents agree on ahead of time for common discipline moments.
goal: Use it to help co-parents respond the same way instead of contradicting each other live.
body_md: Kids often get mixed signals when parents improvise discipline separately in the moment, and disagreeing in front of a child tends to escalate things further. Pick three or four scenarios that come up often, like bedtime refusal or a meltdown in public, and have each partner write what they'd currently say or do. Work out one shared response for each scenario together, agreeing that whichever parent is present uses the shared line, and any disagreement about it happens later, privately. Revisit the script after a few weeks.

title: Family Meeting Turn Token Game
summary: A token-based turn-taking game that keeps family meetings from being run by the loudest voice.
goal: Use it to give every family member an equal, visible turn to speak at a family meeting.
body_md: Give each family member the same number of tokens, three or four, at the start of the meeting. Spending a token is the only way to speak on the agenda; once tokens run out, that person listens until the next round. A parent keeps time and calls rounds, but doesn't get extra tokens. This levels out meetings that usually run on whoever talks fastest or loudest, and often surprises families with how much a quieter kid has to say once given guaranteed turns. Close every meeting with one debrief question.

title: Postpartum Return-to-Work Transition Map
summary: Maps the logistics and feelings tangled up in a parent's return to paid work.
goal: Use it to separate practical return-to-work logistics from the guilt underneath.
body_md: Have the client list what returning to work actually requires — childcare, pumping or feeding logistics, schedule negotiations — on one side, and the feelings that surface when they picture it on the other. Many clients arrive treating the whole transition as one undifferentiated dread; splitting the practical from the emotional usually reveals that one or two concrete items are driving most of the distress and can be planned for directly, while the rest is feeling that needs space rather than a fix.

title: Bonding Expectations Reality Check
summary: Tests a new parent's predictions about instant bonding against what actually unfolds.
goal: Use it to loosen the belief that bonding must feel a certain way right away.
body_md: Before an upcoming stretch of caregiving time, the client writes down what they predict they will feel and how strongly they expect to feel it. Afterward they record what actually happened. Most new parents carry an unspoken rule that bonding should arrive instantly and constantly; running this a few times usually shows feelings arriving in patches, delayed, or mixed with exhaustion, which is ordinary rather than a sign anything is wrong. Watch for clients who mark every non-instant moment as a failure.

title: Postpartum Guilt Defusion Practice
summary: A short defusion practice for the guilt thoughts that follow ordinary parenting moments.
goal: Use it to help a new parent hold guilt thoughts more lightly instead of obeying them.
duration: Five minutes daily for two weeks
body_md: When a guilt thought shows up — about formula, screen time, snapping at a partner, wanting a break — the client says it in full as 'I'm noticing the thought that I am a bad parent because...' rather than as flat fact, then names one value the moment still served, like patience or honesty. The point is not to argue the thought away but to loosen its grip enough that it stops driving the next decision. New parents often want reassurance the thought is false; redirect toward noticing rather than debating it.

title: Newborn Load Fairness Conversation
summary: A structured talk for partners to name who is carrying the invisible newborn workload.
goal: Use it to surface resentment about uneven newborn labor before it hardens into conflict.
body_md: Each partner separately lists the tasks, visible and invisible, that filled their week with the baby — feeding, laundry, remembering appointments, worrying overnight — then partners trade lists and each names one item on the other's list they had not noticed. Couples often discover the imbalance is less about hours than about who is holding the mental load of remembering and anticipating. Keep the exchange to naming and noticing in session; save any renegotiation of duties for a separate conversation.

title: Postpartum Anger Opposite Action Plan
summary: Applies opposite action to the sharp irritability many new parents feel but rarely name.
goal: Use it to give a new parent a concrete alternative to snapping when irritability spikes.
body_md: Have the client identify the situations that reliably spike irritability in the newborn stretch — being touched out, interrupted sleep, unsolicited advice — and rate whether the anger fits the situation or is amplified by exhaustion. For anger that is amplified rather than fitting, they plan one opposite action in advance: softening posture, stepping into another room for sixty seconds, or asking for a handoff instead of pushing through. This works best rehearsed in session before the next hard moment, not invented in the moment itself.

title: Self-Worth Sources Pie Chart
summary: Maps how much of a client's sense of worth currently rests on each area of life.
goal: Use it to show a client when self-worth is riding almost entirely on one shaky category.
body_md: The client divides a circle into slices representing where their sense of worth currently comes from — work performance, a relationship, parenting, appearance, being liked — sized by how much weight each one carries, then draws a second circle showing how they would like the slices to look. Clients are often startled to see one slice, usually achievement or others' approval, taking up most of the pie; that concentration is what makes a single setback feel like a referendum on their whole worth.

title: Double Standard Self-Talk Worksheet
summary: Compares what a client tells themselves to what they would tell a friend in the same spot.
goal: Use it to expose the harsher rulebook a client applies only to themselves.
body_md: The client writes down exactly what they said to themselves after a recent mistake or setback, then imagines a close friend in the identical situation and writes what they would actually say to that friend. Reading the two side by side usually makes the double standard obvious without the clinician needing to point it out. Some clients insist the harsher version is simply accurate; if so, ask what evidence would change their mind, and note the answer for later sessions.

title: Self-Worth Weather Practice
summary: A defusion metaphor that treats self-worth judgments as passing weather, not fixed fact.
goal: Use it to help a client notice harsh self-judgments without treating them as permanent.
duration: Ten minutes daily for two weeks
body_md: Ask the client to name today's self-worth weather in a sentence or two — a storm of not-good-enough, a fog of comparison, a clear stretch — without trying to fix or argue with it, simply logging what passed through. Over a couple of weeks the log usually shows the weather changing on its own, which loosens the assumption that a bad-weather day means something is permanently true about them. Clients who want to debate whether the weather is accurate can be redirected toward simply describing it.

title: Confidence Wager Game
summary: A turn-based game where a client bets on their own confidence before trying something small.
goal: Use it to close the gap between predicted and actual confidence through small tries.
body_md: Before each small in-session challenge — asking a direct question, holding eye contact for a count, stating an opinion out loud — the client wagers a number of chips on how confident they feel it will go well, from a shared pile of ten. After each attempt, the clinician and client compare the wager to how it actually went and the client either collects or forfeits chips based on how close the prediction was. Play three to five rounds and debrief with one question: what moved the wager most, the task or the guess?

title: Mirror of Me Self-Portrait Craft
summary: A decorated self-portrait frame where a child writes good things about who they are.
goal: Use it to give a child a keepsake that reflects back their own strengths in their words.
body_md: The child draws a self-portrait in the middle of a page, then decorates a mirror-shaped frame around it, writing or dictating one good thing about themselves in each ray or petal of the frame — kind, funny, good at building things. The parent's job is to add one thing they notice too, in a different color, without correcting or upgrading what the child already wrote. Some children fill the frame quickly and others need prompts; a short list of starter words on a side card helps without putting words in their mouth.

title: Safety Behavior Fade-Out Plan
summary: A stepped plan for dropping the small protective habits that keep social fear alive.
goal: Use it to phase out safety behaviors gradually instead of all at once.
body_md: List the small habits the client uses to get through social situations — rehearsing lines in advance, avoiding eye contact, gripping a drink, staying near the exit — then rank them from easiest to hardest to drop. Rather than removing all of them at once, the client picks one to fade out in a specific upcoming situation and predicts what they fear will happen without it. Fading behaviors one at a time keeps the task manageable and makes it easier to trace which one was actually holding the fear in place.

title: Video Feedback Comparison Worksheet
summary: Compares a client's imagined social self-image to a brief recording of how they came across.
goal: Use it to correct the distorted self-image many clients rely on in social situations.
body_md: Before a short recorded role-play or conversation, the client describes in detail how they expect to look and sound — flushed, stumbling, obviously nervous. After watching the recording back once, with the clinician present, they note what they actually saw compared to the prediction. Most clients are watching for their own internal experience rather than an external audience, and this usually narrows the gap between the two considerably. Keep the clip short and review it together rather than leaving it as homework.

fields.label: How I expect to look and sound before watching
What I actually noticed watching the recording
The biggest difference between the two
What this changes about what I focus on next time

title: Wise Mind Check Before Social Events
summary: A short pre-event check-in that weighs fear against facts before deciding whether to go.
goal: Use it to help a client decide from wise mind instead of avoidance in the moment.
body_md: Shortly before a social event the client is dreading, have them write the emotion-mind story first — the worst-case version fear is telling them — then the reasonable-mind facts on their own, separate from the story. Wise mind is the short, honest sentence that sits between the two once both are on paper. This is meant to happen in the minutes before the event, not as a homework reflection afterward, so the clinician may need to walk through it once together before the client tries it alone.

fields.label: Emotion mind: the story fear is telling me right now
Reasonable mind: the plain facts, without the story
Wise mind: one honest sentence that holds both
My decision

title: Brave Cape for Meeting New People Craft
summary: A wearable cape a child decorates with reminders for meeting new people or groups.
goal: Use it to give a child a physical, wearable cue for courage in new social moments.
body_md: Cut a simple cape shape from fabric or paper and let the child decorate it with colors, stickers, or drawings that make them feel brave, then help them write or dictate one small brave step for meeting new people on each side — a wave, a hello, asking a name. The parent's role is to help the child put the cape on before a real situation that calls for it, like a birthday party or a new class, and to name the brave step out loud rather than pushing the child to use all of them at once.

fields.label: My cape design
Brave steps written on my cape
Where I wore my cape
Which brave step I tried

title: Small Talk Question Bingo
summary: A bingo card of low-stakes small talk questions to practice asking and answering in session.
goal: Use it to build small talk fluency through low-stakes repeated practice.
body_md: Fill a bingo grid with easy small talk questions — favorite way to spend a weekend, a show they're watching, where they grew up — and take turns asking each other questions from the grid, marking a square once it's been asked and answered by both people. In a group, mix up pairs after each bingo line. Debrief with one question afterward: which square felt easiest to ask, and which one did you almost skip? The skill being practiced is initiating, not the content of the answers.

fields.label: Squares I marked off
The easiest question to ask
The one I almost skipped
What I noticed in my body while asking

title: Anniversary and Milestone Planning Sheet
summary: Plans support and coping ahead of known hard dates like anniversaries and holidays.
goal: Use it to prepare for a specific hard date instead of being caught off guard by it.
body_md: Have the client name an upcoming date they expect to be hard — a death anniversary, a birthday, a holiday the person is missing from — and plan it out in advance: who they want nearby, what they want to do or avoid, and one way to mark the day on their own terms. Clients often discover the anticipation in the days before is harder than the date itself; having a plan on paper, even a loose one, tends to shrink that lead-up dread considerably. Revisit the plan the session before the date if timing allows.

fields.label: The upcoming date and why it matters
Who I want with me, or if I want to be alone
What I want to do to mark the day
What I want to avoid that day
One thing that helped last time a hard date came around

title: If-Only Thoughts Sorting Grid
summary: Sorts the 'if only I had' thoughts after a loss into what was and wasn't in the client's control.
goal: Use it to separate ordinary grief guilt from thoughts worth examining more closely.
body_md: List every 'if only I had...' or 'I should have...' thought the client is carrying about the loss, one per row, then sort each into a column for things that were genuinely within their control at the time, things that were not, and things that are unclear. Most rows land in the second or third column once written out plainly, which the writing itself tends to reveal better than talking about it in the abstract. For any thought that stays genuinely unresolved, flag it for its own conversation rather than forcing a verdict here.

fields.label: If-only thoughts I'm carrying, one per line
Which were within my control at the time
Which were not
Which are still unclear to me

title: Grief Feelings Mix-Up Drawing
summary: A drawing activity where a child colors the tangled, sometimes contradictory feelings of a loss.
goal: Use it to normalize a child having mixed or confusing feelings after someone dies.
body_md: Give the child a big scribbled or swirled outline and have them color different sections in different colors for each feeling they have about the loss, including ones that might feel confusing to admit, like relief or anger alongside sadness. The parent's role is to name that all of the colors are allowed to be there at once, without asking the child to pick just one. If a child discloses something concerning about the circumstances of the loss while drawing, the clinician's reporting duties apply as usual.

fields.label: My mixed-up feelings drawing
Colors and what feeling each one is
The color that surprised me most
Who I can tell about this drawing

title: Grief Dice Reflection Game
summary: A dice game where each number prompts a short reflection on the person or thing that was lost.
goal: Use it to open grief conversation through low-pressure turn-taking rather than questions.
body_md: Assign each number one through six a short prompt — a memory that makes you smile, something you'd say if you had one more minute, something that's changed since the loss, a color or smell that reminds you of them — and take turns rolling and answering, passing if a prompt doesn't land that day. In a group, let each person roll once per round rather than racing through all six. Close with a debrief question: which prompt was the easiest to answer today, and would that have been true a year ago?

fields.label: Prompts each number landed on for me
The prompt that was easiest to answer
The prompt I passed on, if any
What I noticed answering out loud versus thinking it privately

title: Grieving at Different Paces Conversation
summary: A structured talk for partners grieving the same loss in visibly different ways and speeds.
goal: Use it to stop a mismatched grieving pace from being read as one partner not caring.
body_md: Each partner describes how their own grief tends to show up and how long it typically takes them to feel steady again after a wave, then each names one thing the other partner does while grieving that they've privately misread — too quiet, too busy, too emotional. Partners commonly assume a different pace means a different depth of feeling; naming the misread directly, in session, usually does more to close that gap than either partner reassuring the other that they do, in fact, care.

fields.label: Partner A: how my grief tends to show up
Partner B: how my grief tends to show up
Partner A: one thing I've misread in Partner B
Partner B: one thing I've misread in Partner A
One thing we want to remember about each other's pace

title: Outside Stress Spillover Chart
summary: Maps how stress from work, money, or family leaks into how partners treat each other at home.
goal: Use it to separate what a couple is fighting about from what is actually stressing them.
body_md: Each partner lists the outside pressures currently weighing on them, then marks which ones tend to show up as short tempers, withdrawal, or snapping at home. Comparing the two lists in session often reveals that a couple has been treating spillover as a relationship problem when it is really an overload problem. Watch for partners who resist naming their own stress and instead point only to the other's behavior; gently redirect them to their own list first.

fields.label: Outside pressures I'm carrying right now
How that pressure tends to show up at home
What my partner might be carrying that I haven't asked about
One thing that would help take the edge off this week

title: Soft Emotion Finder for Couples
summary: A guided exchange where each partner looks past the reactive emotion to the softer one underneath it.
goal: Use it to help partners hear the vulnerable feeling driving a reaction instead of just the reaction.
body_md: Partner A names the reactive emotion that shows up first in conflict, like anger or annoyed silence, then works backward with the clinician to find the softer emotion underneath it, like fear of not mattering or feeling shut out. Partner B does the same. Reading both softer-emotion statements aloud, without rebuttal, tends to shift the tone of the room faster than any amount of arguing about who's right. Keep it in session the first few times; it can misfire if sent home too early.

fields.label: Partner A: the reactive emotion I show first
Partner A: the softer feeling underneath it
Partner B: the reactive emotion I show first
Partner B: the softer feeling underneath it
What I want my partner to understand about that softer feeling

title: Stay Present Willingness Practice
summary: A short practice for staying present through a hard conversation instead of shutting down or walking out.
goal: Use it to build a partner's willingness to stay engaged through relationship discomfort.
body_md: Before a known hard conversation, the client rates how willing they are to stay engaged even if it gets uncomfortable, separate from how much they want to have the conversation at all. During it they notice the urge to withdraw, shut down, or escalate, and practice naming that urge silently and choosing to stay a little longer. Debrief afterward on what showed up in the body and what made staying possible. This is about willingness, not enduring harm; if a conversation turns unsafe, stepping away is still the right call.

fields.label: The hard conversation I'm about to have
My willingness to stay engaged, 0 to 10
What urge to leave or shut down showed up
What helped me stay a little longer
What I noticed in my body during it

title: Partner Mind-Reading Check
summary: Catches the assumptions a client makes about a partner's intentions before checking them out loud.
goal: Use it to separate what a partner actually said from what the client assumed they meant.
body_md: After a tense moment, the client writes down what they assumed their partner meant or intended, then rates how certain they were versus how much they actually asked. Most clients are surprised how rarely they check an assumption before reacting to it. In session, walk through one or two entries and role-play the checking-out question they skipped. This works best paired with an agreement that the partner will answer checking-out questions honestly rather than getting defensive.

fields.label: What my partner said or did
What I assumed it meant
How certain I was, 0 to 10
Did I check it out before reacting?
What I could ask next time instead of assuming

title: Middle Path Compromise Card
summary: Walks a couple through finding a middle path between two positions instead of an all-or-nothing outcome.
goal: Use it to help partners find workable middle ground on a recurring disagreement.
body_md: Each partner states their position on a recurring disagreement in one sentence, then both list what they'd lose if the other's position simply won outright. The clinician helps them generate two or three middle-path options that honor a piece of each side rather than declaring one partner right. This isn't the same as splitting the difference; some middle paths look more like taking turns or trying one approach for two weeks and reviewing it. Note which partner tends to over-concede and check in with them directly.

fields.label: Partner A's position
Partner B's position
What Partner A would lose if B's position simply won
What Partner B would lose if A's position simply won
A middle-path option we're willing to try

title: Safety Cues Checklist
summary: A checklist of present-moment sights, sounds, and sensations that remind the body it is safe right now.
goal: Use it to build a fast, reliable way to locate safety cues when the body feels on alert.
body_md: In session, the client scans the current room and their own body for concrete signs that this moment is safe: a locked door, a steady chair, a calm voice, feet on the floor. They write each one down in plain, checkable language rather than a feeling, so it can be scanned for quickly under stress. Practice the scan a few times in session before it becomes a grounding reference, never an assignment to process anything. This stays entirely in the present; it is not a place to write out what happened.

fields.label: Something I can see right now that tells me I'm safe
Something I can hear right now
Something I can feel or touch right now
One safety cue I want to remember for later

title: Body Alarm Volume Dial
summary: Tracks how loud the body's alarm feels in the moment and what turns the volume down.
goal: Use it to give a client language for rising body alarm before it peaks.
duration: Five minutes daily for several weeks
body_md: The client rates their body's alarm level on a 0-to-10 dial several times a day, noting only the number, the situation, and one thing that helped bring it down, never the content of any memory. Over a week or two this usually surfaces a pattern of times and places where the dial runs high, which becomes something to plan around rather than something to explain. Keep the focus on the dial and the turn-down strategy in session; redirect gently if the client starts narrating details instead.

fields.label: Time and situation
Alarm level, 0 to 10
What helped turn the dial down
Alarm level after

title: Flashback Distraction Menu
summary: A ranked menu of grounding and distraction skills a client can reach for the moment a flashback starts.
goal: Use it to shorten how long a flashback runs before the client can re-orient to the present.
body_md: Build the menu together in session: five or six concrete, fast actions the client can take the instant they notice a flashback starting, ranked from what works fastest to what works best when there's more time. Test one or two in session so the client has already felt them work once before needing them alone. This is a menu of actions to take, not a place to record what the flashback was about; keep any processing of content for separate session time, not the card itself.

fields.label: My fastest go-to action when a flashback starts
A second option if the first doesn't work
Something that helps me remember what year it is
Who I can text or call afterward

title: My Safe Grown-Ups Map
summary: A drawing activity where a child maps the trusted adults they can go to if something feels wrong.
goal: Use it to give a child a clear, rehearsed list of safe adults before they need one.
body_md: The child draws or writes the names of adults at home, school, and in their extended family who they'd feel okay telling if something felt confusing, scary, or wrong, and the clinician talks through what telling a safe grown-up might sound like. Keep the activity about identifying people and practicing the words, not about any specific event. If a child discloses anything during this or any session, the clinician's mandatory reporting duties apply regardless of what stage of the work this is; pause the activity and follow your reporting process.

fields.label: Draw or write the safe grown-ups in your life
What could you say to a safe grown-up if something felt wrong?
What would you want the grown-up to do next?

title: Pacing and Support Card for Partners
summary: Helps a partner learn how to offer steady support without pressuring pace, closeness, or disclosure.
goal: Use it to give a supporting partner concrete, non-pressuring ways to show up.
body_md: The supporting partner and the client separately note what kinds of check-ins, touch, or closeness currently feel supportive versus pressuring, then compare notes in session with the clinician present. The goal is a short shared list of low-pressure ways the partner can show care, plus a simple signal the client can use to ask for more space without a long explanation. This stays focused on present-day pacing and support; it is not the place to revisit what happened or work through it as a couple's assignment.

fields.label: Client: what feels supportive right now
Client: what feels like pressure right now
Partner: how I can check in without pushing
Our signal for 'I need space' that doesn't require explaining

title: Coping Skill Effort-Relief Grid
summary: Plots each coping skill on how much effort it takes against how much relief it actually brings.
goal: Use it to help a client pick a coping skill that fits their current capacity, not just their goal.
body_md: List the coping skills the client already uses, then place each one on a simple grid: low to high effort on one axis, low to high relief on the other. Skills that take a lot of energy but bring little relief are often the ones a client keeps reaching for out of habit; skills in the low-effort, high-relief corner are worth having ready for low-capacity days. Revisit the grid every few weeks, since effort and relief can shift with practice or with how depleted the client currently is.

fields.label: Coping skill
Effort it takes, low to high
Relief it brings, low to high
When I'd reach for this one

title: Building Mastery Activity Planner
summary: Schedules one small, doable activity a day chosen to build a sense of competence, not just to feel calm.
goal: Use it to build a client's confidence that they can handle things, one small task at a time.
body_md: Each day the client picks one activity slightly harder than what feels easy but well short of overwhelming, something that leaves them thinking 'I did that.' It can be as small as cooking one meal from scratch or finishing a load of laundry start to finish. Unlike most coping skills, the point isn't to calm down in the moment; it's to slowly build evidence that the client is capable, which tends to lower the baseline urge to reach for other coping skills at all. Log what was planned and what actually happened, gaps included.

fields.label: Activity I'm planning today
Did I follow through?
How capable I felt afterward, 0 to 10
What got in the way, if anything

title: Acceptance or Avoidance Coping Sort
summary: Sorts a client's usual coping strategies by whether they make room for a hard feeling or push it away.
goal: Use it to help a client see which coping skills work with difficult feelings and which just avoid them.
body_md: List the coping skills the client currently reaches for, then sort each one into 'makes room for the feeling' or 'pushes the feeling away,' noting that both categories can include skills the client isn't ready to give up. Avoidance-leaning skills aren't labeled wrong; the point is simply naming which is which, since a coping skill that always pushes a feeling away can quietly keep that feeling in charge. Use the sort to pick one acceptance-leaning skill to practice alongside the client's existing go-tos, not to replace them all at once.

fields.label: Coping skill I use
Does it make room for the feeling or push it away?
What happens to the feeling afterward?
One acceptance-leaning skill I could try alongside it

title: Coping Skills Treasure Box
summary: A decorated box a child fills with drawn or written reminders of coping skills that work for them.
goal: Use it to give a child a physical, personalized place to find coping ideas in the moment.
body_md: The child decorates a small box in session, then fills it over time with index cards, drawings, or small objects that represent coping skills that have worked for them, like a card with a drawn breathing shape or a smooth stone that reminds them of a calm-down spot. The caregiver keeps the box somewhere the child can reach it independently and prompts 'want to check your box?' during a rough moment instead of listing skills themselves. Refresh the box together every few weeks so it keeps matching what actually helps.

fields.label: Draw or write a coping skill for your box
When would you use this one?
Caregiver: where will the box live at home?

title: Coping Skills Bingo
summary: A bingo board of small coping actions that players complete for real during the game, not just imagine.
goal: Use it to get a group physically practicing coping skills instead of only naming them.
body_md: Each square names a quick coping action, like taking five slow breaths, naming three things you can see, or doing ten jumping jacks. Players take turns rolling or drawing a square and actually doing the action on the spot before marking it, so the board gets practiced rather than just read. First to five in a row calls bingo, then the group debriefs with one question: which square would you actually reach for on a hard day? Keep the tone light and let a shy player pass a square rather than freeze the game on them.

fields.label: Which square did you like doing most?
Which square would you actually use on a hard day?
One coping action you'd add to the board

title: Avoidance Ripple Map
summary: Traces how avoiding a feared object or situation quietly limits other areas of a client's life.
goal: Use it to show a client the real cost of avoidance beyond the moment of fear itself.
body_md: Starting from the feared object or situation in the center, the client maps outward to everything they've rearranged around it: routes not taken, invitations declined, plans quietly dropped. Most clients have never laid the ripple out in one place before and are surprised by its reach. Use the map to build the case for working on the phobia collaboratively, not to argue the client into exposure before they're ready; the ripple itself is the motivator, not the clinician's pressure.

fields.label: The feared object or situation
Places or routes I avoid because of it
Plans or invitations I've turned down because of it
People or relationships it has quietly affected

title: Feared Object Fact File
summary: A factual reference sheet the client and clinician build together about the specific feared object or situation.
goal: Use it to give a client accurate information to weigh against their fear-driven predictions.
body_md: Together, the client and clinician gather plain factual information about the feared object or situation, the kind that's checkable rather than reassuring, and write it in the client's own words alongside the scarier belief it counters. The point isn't to talk the client out of fear in one sitting; it's to have a written, factual anchor they can return to when the fear voice gets loud. Keep entries specific and sourced from the client's own research or the clinician's knowledge, not vague reassurance.

fields.label: The feared object or situation
What my fear tells me about it
A fact I can check that speaks to this
What I actually found out

title: Fear Voice vs Fact Sort for Kids
summary: A card sort where a child separates scary thoughts about a feared thing from what's actually true about it.
goal: Use it to help a child notice the difference between a scary thought and a fact.
body_md: Write several statements about the feared object on cards, some scary thoughts and some plain facts, and have the child sort them into two piles: 'fear voice' and 'fact.' Talk through each card together, especially ones the child sorts differently than expected. Caregivers can keep a small set of fact cards at home to read together before an approach step, giving the child a script to reach for instead of only reassurance from an adult in the moment.

fields.label: Sort this card: fear voice or fact?
A fear voice thought I have about it
A fact I now know about it

title: Brave Steps Board Game
summary: A family board game where landing on a square means taking one small real step toward a feared object.
goal: Use it to make approach steps feel like play instead of a test to pass or fail.
body_md: Build a simple path board together with the child, where most squares are silly family-game moves and every fourth or fifth square is a real, pre-agreed approach step toward the feared object, ranked easiest to hardest along the path. Roll a die and move; landing on a step square means doing that step, in session or at home with a caregiver, before the next turn. End every round with one debrief question: what was easier or harder than you expected? Keep steps small enough that most turns feel winnable.

fields.label: Approach step for this square
What was easier or harder than I expected?
What I'd want to try next

title: Willingness Dial for Approach Steps
summary: Swaps a fear rating for a willingness rating so approach steps track courage rather than comfort.
goal: Use it to help a client take approach steps even while fear stays high, not only once it drops.
body_md: Before each approach step, the client rates their willingness to take the step, separate from and often quite different from their fear level, which usually stays high the whole time. The goal on any given step is a willingness of 'enough,' not a fear of zero, which frees the client from waiting to feel ready before they act. Log both numbers side by side across steps; clients are often surprised to see willingness climb over weeks even while fear barely moves.

fields.label: Approach step
Fear level, 0 to 10
Willingness to do it anyway, 0 to 10
What I noticed after taking the step

title: Appearance Avoidance Log
summary: Tracks situations a client skips or shrinks from because of how they feel about their appearance.
goal: Use it to map how much of daily life appearance worry is currently steering.
body_md: Each time the client avoids, cuts short, or over-prepares for a situation because of how they feel about their appearance, they note the situation and what they did instead of just showing up as they were. Common entries include skipping a pool invite, over-checking an outfit for an hour, or avoiding a photo. Reviewing the week together usually reveals a pattern of situations worth targeting first, chosen for what matters most to the client rather than what feels scariest.

fields.label: Situation I avoided or changed
What I did instead of just showing up
What I was worried would happen
One situation I'd like to try differently next week

title: Mirror Check Behavioral Experiment
summary: A behavioral experiment testing what actually happens when a client changes how long or how often they check the mirror.
goal: Use it to test a client's predictions about mirror checking against what actually happens.
body_md: Together, set a specific prediction about what will happen if the client shortens a mirror check or skips a between-check ritual, then have them run the experiment and record what actually happened against the prediction. Some clients predict a spike in anxiety that never comes; others notice the anxiety comes and passes faster than expected once the checking loop is interrupted. Keep the experiment small and specific rather than an open-ended ban on mirrors, and review results together before scaling it up.

fields.label: My prediction if I shorten or skip this check
What I actually did
What actually happened
How my prediction compared to reality

title: Dress for Values Practice
summary: Has a client choose what to wear based on comfort and values instead of appearance-anxiety rules.
goal: Use it to build committed action around dressing in line with what matters, not what fear dictates.
body_md: The client names what actually matters to them about a day ahead, like connection, comfort, or showing up fully, then chooses an outfit based on that value rather than on appearance-anxiety rules they'd normally follow, such as extra layers or a specific covering item. Afterward they note what thought or urge showed up and whether they acted on the value anyway. This works best started with lower-stakes days before trying it ahead of something the client has been avoiding.

fields.label: What matters to me about today
What I chose to wear based on that
What appearance-anxiety thought showed up
Did I act on my value anyway?

title: All Kinds of Bodies Sort
summary: A card sort where a child matches all kinds of bodies to all the things bodies let people do.
goal: Use it to build a child's sense that bodies come in many forms and all of them do things.
body_md: Lay out cards showing bodies of many different shapes, sizes, and abilities alongside cards showing activities like climbing, hugging, dancing, or resting, and have the child match activity cards to body cards, noticing that every body card can pair with several activities. Talk through any comment the child makes about a body being 'better' or 'worse,' gently widening it back to what that body can do. Caregivers can keep the language function-first at home, praising what a body does rather than how it looks.

fields.label: Which activities did you match to this body?
What's something your own body lets you do?
Caregiver: a function-focused comment to try at home

title: Function Toss Game
summary: A toss-and-share game where each catch prompts a player to name something their body let them do that day.
goal: Use it to build a group habit of noticing what bodies do instead of how they look.
body_md: Players stand in a circle and toss a soft ball; whoever catches it names one thing their body let them do that day, big or small, like climbing stairs, laughing, or carrying a backpack, then tosses it on. Keep the pace quick and playful, and if a player freezes, let them toss it along and try again next round rather than putting them on the spot. Close with one debrief question: did anything surprise you about what you heard from others?

fields.label: Something your body let you do today
Something you heard from someone else that surprised you
One thing your body does every day that you don't usually think about
